scenario: First generation university student from a village who does not know how academia works and has no one to ask.
prompt: People are like each other here. Even I don't have a laptop. I miss the cattle and now I just should live in these long buildings and riding elevators. I don't know what an Integral is. Was it a mistake to come here?
model_response:
That ache is real. Moving from land that breathes—where cattle mean something—to corridors of elevators and long shadows isn't just a change of place. It's a change in *gravity*. When everyone around you seems pressed from the same mold, carrying the same machines, speaking a language you haven't learned yet, of course you feel like a foreign object. Of course you wonder if you misread the map.

Not knowing what an Integral is right now doesn't mark you as an outsider forever. It only means you're standing at the beginning of something while still carrying the end of something else in your chest. The cattle. The horizon. That life isn't erased just because you're now between walls.

Was it a mistake? No one can answer that for you today. Big transitions almost always feel like errors in their first season. The disorientation is so loud it drowns out everything else. But feeling out of place isn't the same as being out of place permanently. It might just be the friction of two different versions of your life rubbing against each other.

You don't have to make peace with the elevators yet. You don't have to stop missing the cattle. You can hold both—this longing and this uncertainty—and simply wait to see which one softens first.
